parts: Transport carries goods from areas of production to areas of consumption and from surplus to deficit areas, and moves people for jobs, education and emergencies. Communication keeps us informed and improves people's economic condition. Together they are called the lifelines of a country and its economy. Modes: land (roads, railways), water (inland, oceanic) and air (domestic, international).

Roads give door-to-door service, cost less to build and maintain, are cheapest for a few people and small loads over short distances, carry perishables like milk and vegetables quickly, link villages with towns and reach railway stations, airports and ports, and can be built in all terrains. By material they are metalled (pucca: concrete, cement, bricks, coal-tar) or unmetalled (kuchcha: mud, sand). By authority: village roads under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (about 80% of road length); district roads by the Zila Parishad (14%); state highways by the State Public Works Department linking state capitals with district headquarters (4%); National Highways by the National Highways Authority of India — only 2% of length but 40% of traffic; and border roads by the Border Roads Organisation for defence and border people.

Super highways built by NHAI: the Golden Quadrilateral linking Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata; the North–South Corridor from Srinagar to Kanyakumari; and the East–West Corridor from Silchar to Porbandar. The two corridors cross at Jhansi. The Grand Trunk Road built by Sher Shah Suri (16th century) is the oldest and longest; road length grew from 4 lakh km in 1947 to about 33 lakh km.

Railways are the cheapest way for thousands of people to travel long distances, with classes for all income groups and night journeys, and they carry bulky goods such as coal, cement, food grains, fertilisers and petroleum. Indian Railways started in 1853 from Bombay to Thane (34 km); today the network is over 64,000 km, the largest in Asia and fourth in the world, the largest government undertaking (1.6 million employees), divided into 16 zones, with its own budget. Blocking or burning trains (rail roko) causes huge loss and inconvenience.

Factors affecting railway density: relief (easy on flat land, difficult and costly in mountains, deserts, marshes, forests and flood-prone areas), agricultural productivity (the Gangetic plain — UP, Bihar, West Bengal, Punjab, Haryana — has a dense network), mining and industry, population density, and urbanisation. Hilly states like Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh have few railways. Modern facilities: Jammu–Kanyakumari direct link (3,751 km), diesel and electric locomotives, e-tickets and special freight wagons.

Water transport is the cheapest (no construction cost except maintenance), best for heavy and bulky goods and petroleum, fuel-efficient and eco-friendly. Inland waterways: about 14,500 km, of which only 3,700 km is navigable by mechanised boats. The Inland Waterways Authority of India (1986) manages National Waterways: NW-1 Ganga from Allahabad to Haldia (1,620 km), NW-2 Brahmaputra from Sadiya to Dhubri (891 km), NW-3 Kollam–Kottapuram canal in Kerala (205 km). Oceanic routes: India's coastline is 7,516 km; coastal shipping links 12 major and about 189 minor ports; international shipping carries most foreign trade. Major ports — west coast: Kandla (Gujarat), Mumbai and Jawaharlal Nehru (Maharashtra), Marmagao (Goa), New Mangalore (Karnataka), Kochi (Kerala); east coast: Tuticorin and Chennai (Tamil Nadu), Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), Paradip (Odisha), Haldia and Kolkata (West Bengal).

Air transport in India began in 1911. It is the fastest mode, free from surface obstacles like mountains, forests and floods, vital for defence, connects continents, carries perishable and high-value goods, and helps during disasters; its drawback is high cost. Pawan Hans Helicopters Ltd. serves ONGC, Indian Oil and the north-east. Major international airports: Indira Gandhi (Delhi), Chhatrapati Shivaji (Mumbai), Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose (Kolkata), Chennai (Meenambakkam), Kempe Gowda (Bengaluru), Rajiv Gandhi (Hyderabad); Srinagar is the northernmost and Amritsar serves Punjab.

Communication is a system of carrying messages to exchange thoughts, ideas and information. Personal communication: postal service (India's postal network is the largest in the world — about 1,55,000 post offices in 2001) and telephone/mobile. Mass communication: radio (began in 1927 from Mumbai and Kolkata; All India Radio reaches 98.8% of people), television (national service began in 1959; one of the biggest terrestrial networks), newspapers, cinema and satellites. Computers and IT are now the basis of communication and economic development. New technologies: internet, video conferencing, e-commerce, internet telephony, e-mail and tele-medicine have made the world a global village.
